passage:
After the college fest in Delhi, Pradeep, sixteen, and his friend Eshaan walked to the metro.
“Did you see Ritika pull her hand away when I held it during the song?” Eshaan grinned. “She was just being shy. Next time I'll try again.”
Pradeep stopped. “Bro, she pulled away. That's a no.”
“She didn't say no.”
“She didn't say yes either. Remember what the health teacher said? Only a clear yes is a yes. Pulling away, going quiet, looking uncomfortable, all of that means stop.”
Eshaan was quiet for a while. “So what do I do?”
“Ask her. Properly. And if she says no, that's the answer.”
Eshaan kicked a stone. “Okay. Yeah. I didn't think of it like that.”

qa.q: What did Ritika do when Eshaan held her hand?
qa.a: She pulled her hand away.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel after Pradeep explained?
qa.a: Eshaan felt a bit embarrassed and thoughtful, realising Ritika had been misread.

qa.q: What did Pradeep say about consent that Eshaan should remember?
qa.a: Only a clear yes is a yes, and pulling away or looking uncomfortable means stop.

qa.q: How might Ritika feel if Eshaan asks her properly and respects her answer?
qa.a: She would likely feel respected and safer around Eshaan, whatever her answer is.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old explains to a friend that consent needs a clear yes and that pulling away means no.

passage:
“Shalini-didi, can I ask you something embarrassing?”
“I'm a nurse, Aadhya. Nothing embarrasses me.”
Aadhya, sixteen, lowered her voice. “Girls at school say you can't get infections the first time. And that contraception makes you sick.”
Shalini put down her tea. “Both wrong. Infections can pass any time. Condoms help protect against pregnancy and many infections. Other methods exist too, but a doctor should explain those, depending on the person.”
“Okay.”
“And the most important thing isn't any of that. It's that nobody should pressure you. If you're not sure, the answer is no. You can change your mind any time.”
Aadhya nodded slowly. “Can I come to you if I have more questions?”
“Always. Or to the clinic. Never just the internet.”

qa.q: What is Shalini's job?
qa.a: She is a nurse.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel asking her question?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and a bit nervous, lowering her voice.

qa.q: Where does Shalini suggest Aadhya go with questions, and why?
qa.a: To her or to the clinic, never just the internet, because they can give accurate information.

qa.q: How might Shalini feel when Aadhya asks if she can come back?
qa.a: She probably feels trusted and glad Aadhya feels safe asking her.

grounding: An older cousin who is a nurse corrects myths and teaches a teenager about consent and sexual health.

passage:
Last winter, my friend Gargi's grandmother died. At school the next week, Gargi looked so lost that I went to hug her in the corridor, arms already open.
She stepped back. “Not now. Please.”
I'm Zeenat. For a second I felt hurt. I only wanted to help. Then I remembered what our counsellor said in the consent session: a no is a full answer, even from a friend, even when you mean well.
So I dropped my arms. “Okay. I'm here if you want anything.”
She nodded. At lunch, she came and sat next to me, silently, and leaned her head on my shoulder for a minute.
That was her choice. It meant more because it was.

qa.q: What did Gargi say when Zeenat went to hug her?
qa.a: “Not now. Please.”

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel when Gargi stepped back?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt for a second, having only wanted to help.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do that showed respect for Gargi's boundary?
qa.a: Zeenat dropped the hug, offered to be there, and let Gargi choose when to come close.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel about Zeenat respecting her no?
qa.a: She likely felt safe and cared for, which is why she chose to lean on Zeenat later.

grounding: A teenager learns that consent and respecting no apply even to kind gestures between friends.

I'm Suraj, and I've sat next to Nazia in class since Class 8. This year she started going out with a senior.
At first she seemed happy. Then things changed. She stopped coming to the library after school; he didn't like her being with boys. She changed her dress for the farewell because he said it was “too much.” Once I saw him take her phone and scroll through it while she stood there.
One day she was crying on the stairs. I sat down. She said, “He says he only does it because he loves me.”
“Love doesn't check your phone,” I said.
She told me more. I said, “Let's go to Ma'am now.” Ms Kapoor, our counsellor, listened to her for an hour, and called Nazia's mother that same evening.

qa.a: Because he didn't like her being with boys.

qa.q: How did Nazia seem to feel when Suraj found her on the stairs?
qa.a: She seemed upset and confused, crying and trying to believe the control was love.

qa.q: What did Suraj do that was helpful?
qa.a: Suraj listened, named the behaviour as not love, and took her to the counsellor the same day.

qa.q: How did Ms Kapoor respond to Nazia?
qa.a: She listened to her for an hour and called Nazia's mother that same evening.

April: His older sister Sana overheard him on the phone telling Ayesha not to go to her cousin's party. After he hung up, Sana said, “That's control, Imran. You're doing to her what you'd hate someone doing to you.” He argued, then went silent.
May: He met Ayesha at the park. “I was wrong. I don't need your password. You can go where you want. If I feel jealous, that's mine to deal with.”
Ayesha looked at him for a long time. “Thank you,” she said. “I was starting to feel scared of you.”

Kalyani, you asked why I didn't like the way that boy kept calling you. Let your Mridul Mama tell you something he's not proud of.

passage:
I'm Omkar, Kalyani's brother. When our Nani died in October, Kalyani, fifteen, didn't cry at the funeral. Everyone said she was strong.
But after that, she stopped eating dinner with us. She kept Nani's grey shawl on her bed and slept wrapped in it. Some nights I heard her talking softly, as if to someone.
One Sunday, Amma found her in the garden, planting a tulsi cutting from Nani's old pot. Kalyani said, “Nani watered this every morning. Someone has to.”
Amma knelt beside her, and they both cried then, finally.
Now every morning Kalyani waters the plant before school. I don't know what she says to it. But she eats dinner with us again.

qa.q: What did Kalyani plant in the garden?
qa.a: A tulsi cutting from Nani's old pot.

qa.q: How was Kalyani feeling in the weeks after the funeral?
qa.a: She was grieving deeply and quietly, missing Nani even though she didn't cry at first.

qa.q: What helped Kalyani begin to mourn?
qa.a: Planting and caring for Nani's tulsi gave her a way to remember Nani and let her finally cry with Amma.

qa.q: How might Amma feel crying with Kalyani in the garden?
qa.a: She probably feels sad but closer to her daughter, sharing their grief at last 🤍

grounding: A brother observes his sister's quiet grief for their grandmother and how she finds a way to mourn.

passage:
Tuesday: Zubin, the old brown dog Joseph, fourteen, had grown up with, didn't wake up. Joseph sat by the basket all morning and wouldn't go to school. He didn't speak all day.
The next Sunday: Joseph found Zubin's red collar behind the sofa. He held it and cried so hard his mother came running. She sat and cried with him.
A month later: Joseph made a small photo book: Zubin as a puppy, Zubin stealing chapatis, Zubin asleep on his school bag. He and his father planted a guava tree in the corner of the yard where Zubin used to lie in the sun.
Joseph still misses him. But he can talk about him now and laugh at the chapati stories.

qa.q: What did Joseph find behind the sofa?
qa.a: Zubin's red collar.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when he found the collar?

qa.q: What helped Joseph mourn Zubin?

passage:
Minakshi, come, sit by your Pooja Dadi. I know you haven't slept since your classmate's funeral. Let me tell you something.
When I was sixteen, my best friend Shobha died of a fever. One week she was laughing with me by the well, and the next she was gone. I stopped talking. I wouldn't eat.

But the truth was, I checked my phone every hour, hoping someone from my old school would message. I felt hollow at night.

I'd lie in bed at eleven, wide awake, and scroll until two. Then I'd drag myself up at six for tuition. By afternoon I was a zombie. I thought I was just lazy.

At the college fest in Pune, Aparna, seventeen, and her friend Tenzin were watching the band when a group of seniors called them over. A cooler of beer was open on the grass.
“Here, juniors.” A can was held out.
Aparna had thought about this moment. She'd read about how alcohol affects the body at her age, and she didn't want to feel out of control somewhere unfamiliar.

Tenzin, who had reached for a can, paused, then put it back. “Me too. I've got practice at six.”

qa.q: How might Tenzin have been affected by Aparna's refusal?
qa.a: Seeing her say no made it easier for Tenzin to refuse too.

grounding: A seventeen-year-old understands the risks of alcohol and refuses it easily at a college fest.

Amandeep, you asked how I ended up doing commerce and music. My family is all engineers. Since I was ten, it was “Eshaan will go to IIT.”
In Class 10, I did the school aptitude test. It said I was strong in numbers and in music, not so much in spatial problems. I'd been playing tabla since I was six. My guru said I had something.

I'm Saurabh, Hansa's older brother. When Hansa, sixteen, had to choose her stream last year, the whole family had opinions.
Nani wanted her to be a doctor. Papa said commerce was safer. Hansa said nothing at the dinner table.
But I saw her at night, reading about nursing on her phone. She'd volunteered at the health camp in our colony and came home glowing, talking about how the nurses calmed scared children.
One evening she asked me, “Is it wrong if I don't want to be a doctor, but I want to be a nurse?”
I said, “Tell them what you told me.”
She did, at dinner, shaking a little. Nani was surprised. Papa asked questions. They agreed she'd take Science with Biology and visit a nursing college first.

I'm Tanuja, Reena's aunt. Last week, while Reena, seventeen, was helping me cook, her phone rang.
“Hello, I'm calling from your bank. Your account will be blocked. Tell me the OTP we just sent.”
Reena's face tightened. “I'll call my bank directly from the number on my card,” she said, and hung up.
I asked how she knew. She shrugged. “Banks never ask for OTPs. Our teacher told us.”
Later she showed me her small notebook. Every rupee from her pocket money and tuition income was written down: phone recharge, bus pass, a birthday gift. At the bottom she'd written what was left and circled it.
I don't remember being that careful at her age.

qa.q: What did the caller ask Reena for?
qa.a: The OTP they just sent.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when she heard the caller's request?
qa.a: She felt suspicious and alert, her face tightening.

qa.q: What safe steps did Reena take with money?
qa.a: She refused to share the OTP, planned to call the bank directly, and kept a notebook of her spending.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Reena's carefulness?
qa.a: Tanuja is impressed, feeling Reena is more careful than she was at that age.

grounding: An aunt observes a seventeen-year-old spot a phone fraud and keep a simple budget.

First week of term: Gurpreet, seventeen, got his first debit card and a payment app. By Friday, half his month's allowance had gone on canteen snacks and late-night food orders. He hadn't noticed until the balance message came.
Two weeks later: His friend Lokesh got a message from a stranger: Scan this QR code to receive ₹2,000 for your old phone. Lokesh was about to scan. Gurpreet stopped him. “You scan to pay, not to receive. That's a trick.” They blocked the number.

Payal, you think these phone frauds only catch old people? Let your Bidisha Pishi tell you.
When I was a clerk at the bank in Kolkata, a young man came in one morning, maybe nineteen, white in the face. He'd got a call saying he'd won a scholarship. To release it, he just had to share the code on his phone. He did. His savings from tuition teaching were gone in a minute.
He kept saying, “It sounded so real.”
That same week, an old lady came to my counter wanting to transfer money to a “nephew” she'd never met. I asked her to wait and call her daughter first. She did. It was a fraud.
No bank or scholarship will ever ask for your code, Payal. When in doubt, stop and ask someone you trust.

qa.q: What did the young man think he had won?
qa.a: A scholarship.

qa.q: How did the young man feel after losing his savings?
qa.a: He felt shocked and devastated, white in the face.

qa.q: What choice inside the story stopped a fraud?
qa.a: Bidisha asking the old lady to wait and call her daughter before transferring the money.

qa.q: How might the old lady have felt after calling her daughter?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and grateful that Bidisha stopped her in time.

grounding: An aunt tells her niece about digital payment frauds she saw at the bank and how to avoid them.

At the school civics club, Zubin, sixteen, held up his phone. “Look, a forwarded message says the candidate from Ward 12 promised free laptops for every student.”
Tejas, the club secretary, frowned. “Where's it from?”
“My uncle's group.”
They checked. The candidate's own printed pamphlet, which Tejas had collected, said nothing about laptops. The local newspaper's interview didn't either. The message had no source, no date.
Zubin felt his face go hot. He'd already forwarded it to three friends.
He messaged them: That laptop thing is not confirmed. Sorry.
In the mock election that afternoon, the club made a rule: every claim on the board needs a source.

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim?
qa.a: That the candidate from Ward 12 promised free laptops for every student.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when he realised the message was false?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face going hot, because he had already forwarded it.

qa.q: What did Zubin and Tejas do to check the claim?
qa.a: They compared it with the candidate's printed pamphlet and the newspaper interview, and noticed it had no source.

qa.q: How might Zubin's friends feel getting his correction?
qa.a: They may appreciate his honesty and be more careful about forwards too.

grounding: A sixteen-year-old learns to check a political claim before sharing and helps set a source rule.

Dear Hansa,
You asked me how voting works because you're doing a project. I voted for the first time last month, so here's what I learned.
Before the day, I checked my name on the voter list online. At the booth in our school, an officer checked my ID, put ink on my finger, and I pressed a button on the machine next to the candidate I chose. A little slip showed my choice for a few seconds, then dropped into a box. Nobody could see who I voted for.
The week before, a video went round claiming one candidate had been arrested. I checked two newspapers. Neither reported it. It was fake.
My advice: read more than one source, and look at what candidates actually promise.
Your cousin, Gargi

Vandana, you asked how I got interested in politics. It wasn't the TV debates. They just made me angry.
At seventeen, our municipal councillor held an open meeting about the broken drains in our ward. My mother dragged me along. I'm Gautam, and I expected shouting.
Instead, I saw how things actually work. The councillor explained which money comes from the state and which from the city. An engineer showed the plan. Residents asked hard questions. The councillor promised a date, and wrote it on a board.
Three months later, the drains were done. I went back to the next meeting on my own.
Now I read two newspapers that disagree with each other every morning. I don't trust any single one.

qa.a: Gautam felt angry and put off by them.

qa.a: How local government actually works, which led Gautam to read two newspapers that disagree, instead of trusting one.

qa.a: The councillor may feel encouraged that a young person is taking an interest.
